paragraphs.text: בִּשְׁנַ֨ת בֹּ֤א תַרְתָּן֙ אַשְׁדּ֔וֹדָה בִּשְׁלֹ֣ח אֹת֔וֹ סַֽרְג֖וֹן מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֑וּר וַיִּלָּ֥חֶם בְּאַשְׁדּ֖וֹד וַֽיִּלְכְּדָֽהּ׃

i18n.en: In the year that the Tartan came to Ashdod, when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him, and he fought against Ashdod and took it,
i18n.he: בִּשְׁנַ֨ת בֹּ֤א תַרְתָּן֙ אַשְׁדּ֔וֹדָה בִּשְׁלֹ֣ח אֹת֔וֹ סַֽרְג֖וֹן מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֑וּר וַיִּלָּ֥חֶם בְּאַשְׁדּ֖וֹד וַֽיִּלְכְּדָֽהּ׃

notes.official:
*Tartān* is not a personal name but the Assyrian title *turtānu* (also *tartānu*), the highest military office below the king, roughly “commander-in-chief” (CAD T s.v. *turtānu*; recalled, the article was not checked). The same title heads the list of Assyrian officers at 2 Kgs 18:17. ASV and JPS 1917 print “Tartan” as a name. The line follows NJPS, “the Tartan,” whose note explains the word as “an Assyrian title meaning ‘General’” (checked on Sefaria). The Hebrew has no article, as is usual with foreign titles used like names (*rab-šāqēh*, 2 Kgs 18:17). The English article is supplied so that the word reads as the title it is (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-20`).

*Sargôn* is Sargon II of Assyria (722–705 BCE), named only here in the Hebrew Bible. His inscriptions record the capture of Ashdod after the revolt of its ruler Yamani, an event usually dated 712 or 711 BCE. They also record that Yamani fled toward Egypt and was handed back by the king of Meluḫḫa, the Assyrian name for Kush (recalled from the standard editions; the wording was not checked). The date, and the help Philistia expected from the Nile, are the background of the sign in 20:2–6. The names take the English and ASV forms (Assyria, Ashdod, Sargon) under overlay `aram-names-isaiah`. The verse is a temporal clause, and the sentence continues into 20:2, as in ASV and JPS 1917.

paragraphs.translit: bišnat bōʾ tartān ʾašdōdāh bišlōaḥ ʾōtō sargōn melek ʾaššūr wayyillāḥem bəʾašdōd wayyilkədāh

paragraphs.text: בָּעֵ֣ת הַהִ֗יא דִּבֶּ֣ר יְהוָה֮ בְּיַ֣ד יְשַׁעְיָ֣הוּ בֶן־אָמוֹץ֮ לֵאמֹר֒ לֵ֗ךְ וּפִתַּחְתָּ֤ הַשַּׂק֙ מֵעַ֣ל מָתְנֶ֔יךָ וְנַעַלְךָ֥ תַחֲלֹ֖ץ מֵעַ֣ל רַגְלֶ֑יךָ וַיַּ֣עַשׂ כֵּ֔ן הָלֹ֖ךְ עָר֥וֹם וְיָחֵֽף׃ (ס)

i18n.en: at that time YHWH spoke by Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying: “Go, and loose the sackcloth from off your loins, and take off your sandals from your feet.” And he did so, walking naked and barefoot.
i18n.he: בָּעֵ֣ת הַהִ֗יא דִּבֶּ֣ר יְהוָה֮ בְּיַ֣ד יְשַׁעְיָ֣הוּ בֶן־אָמוֹץ֮ לֵאמֹר֒ לֵ֗ךְ וּפִתַּחְתָּ֤ הַשַּׂק֙ מֵעַ֣ל מָתְנֶ֔יךָ וְנַעַלְךָ֥ תַחֲלֹ֖ץ מֵעַ֣ל רַגְלֶ֑יךָ וַיַּ֣עַשׂ כֵּ֔ן הָלֹ֖ךְ עָר֥וֹם וְיָחֵֽף׃ (ס)

notes.official:
*Dibber YHWH bᵉyaḏ yᵉšaʿyāhû*, literally “YHWH spoke by the hand of Isaiah”: *bᵉyaḏ* is the idiom for speaking through a messenger or prophet (e.g. Exod 9:35; 1 Kgs 16:7). The line keeps “spoke by Isaiah” with ASV and JPS 1917. The command that follows is addressed to Isaiah himself, so NJPS renders “had spoken to Isaiah.” NJPS also reads *bāʿēṯ hahîʾ* “at that time” as a pluperfect, “Previously,” with the note “Lit. ‘At that time’” (checked on Sefaria): the act began before the year of 20:1, and 20:3 interprets it. The English keeps the literal “at that time,” which allows either sequence.

*Wᵉnaʿalᵉḵā taḥălōṣ mēʿal raḡlêḵā*: the Hebrew has a singular noun, “your sandal,” with the plural “your feet.” The same singular stands in Josh 5:15. It is taken as a collective, and the line has “your sandals,” the book’s word for *naʿal* (5:27), with NJPS. ASV and JPS 1917 put both nouns in the singular (“put thy shoe from off thy foot”). The *śaq* is the coarse garment of mourning and of the prophet. Removing only this garment leaves Isaiah *ʿārôm wᵉyāḥēp̄*, “naked and barefoot,” with ASV, JPS 1917 and NJPS. The adjective can describe a person stripped of the outer garment rather than wholly unclothed (cf. 1 Sam 19:24; Mic 1:8, the prophet going “stripped and naked” in lament; the sense is recognised in the lexica, recalled from BDB and not re-checked). The pair is rendered the same way all three times (20:2, 3, 4), and the choice between the two senses is left to the reader, as in the Hebrew.

paragraphs.translit: bāʿēt hahīʾ dibber YHWH bəyad yəšaʿyāhū ben-ʾāmōṣ lēʾmōr lēk ūpittaḥtā haśśaq mēʿal motnêkā wənaʿalkā taḥălōṣ mēʿal raglêkā wayyaʿaś kēn hālōk ʿārōm wəyāḥēp

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְהוָ֔ה כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר הָלַ֛ךְ עַבְדִּ֥י יְשַׁעְיָ֖הוּ עָר֣וֹם וְיָחֵ֑ף שָׁלֹ֤שׁ שָׁנִים֙ א֣וֹת וּמוֹפֵ֔ת עַל־מִצְרַ֖יִם וְעַל־כּֽוּשׁ׃

i18n.en: And YHWH said: “As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot three years for a sign and a wonder concerning Egypt and concerning Cush,
i18n.he: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְהוָ֔ה כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר הָלַ֛ךְ עַבְדִּ֥י יְשַׁעְיָ֖הוּ עָר֣וֹם וְיָחֵ֑ף שָׁלֹ֤שׁ שָׁנִים֙ א֣וֹת וּמוֹפֵ֔ת עַל־מִצְרַ֖יִם וְעַל־כּֽוּשׁ׃

notes.official:
*ʾôṯ ûmôp̄ēṯ* “a sign and a wonder” is the singular of the pair at 8:18, which the book renders “for signs and for wonders” (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-8`, extended here). ASV and JPS 1917 have “a sign and a wonder”; NJPS has “a sign and a portent.” *Môp̄ēṯ* here is an act that foreshadows an event, a token of what is coming, the same sense as at 8:18 and at Ezek 12:6, 11; 24:24, 27, where the prophet himself is the *môp̄ēṯ*. The Hebrew has no preposition. ASV supplies “for,” and the line keeps it.

The accents put the main break (*ʾaṯnāḥ*) on *wᵉyāḥēp̄*, so *šālōš šānîm* “three years” belongs with what follows: the three years may describe the sign, not the walking. JPS 1917 follows the accents (“to be for three years a sign and a wonder”). NJPS attaches the years to the walking (“has gone naked and barefoot for three years”), and ASV’s order, kept in the line, is ambiguous. The LXX is reported to read “three years shall be signs and wonders” (not verified). Commentators also differ over whether Isaiah went unclothed continuously for three years, or at intervals during a three-year period that matched the time left before the Assyrian blow (both readings are found in the commentary tradition; no single modern work was checked).

*ʿal-miṣrayim wᵉʿal-kûš* is “concerning Egypt and concerning Cush” with ASV. The draft’s “upon” is the wording of JPS 1917; NJPS has “for Egypt and Nubia”; “against” is also possible. *Kûš* is “Cush,” the Nile kingdom south of Egypt, whose Kushite (25th) dynasty ruled Egypt in these years. The form is the book’s (11:11; 43:3; 45:14) under overlay `cush-names-isaiah`. ASV and JPS 1917 print “Ethiopia,” after the LXX *Aithiopia*, and NJPS prints “Nubia.” YHWH’s speech opens here and closes at the end of 20:6, with the coastland’s words in 20:6 as an inner quotation. JPS 1917 and NJPS mark the same extent (checked on Sefaria).

paragraphs.translit: wayyōʾmer YHWH kaʾăšer hālak ʿabdī yəšaʿyāhū ʿārōm wəyāḥēp šālōš šānīm ʾōt ūmōpēt ʿal-miṣrayim wəʿal-kūš

paragraphs.text: כֵּ֣ן יִנְהַ֣ג מֶֽלֶךְ־אַ֠שּׁוּר אֶת־שְׁבִ֨י מִצְרַ֜יִם וְאֶת־גָּל֥וּת כּ֛וּשׁ נְעָרִ֥ים וּזְקֵנִ֖ים עָר֣וֹם וְיָחֵ֑ף וַחֲשׂוּפַ֥י שֵׁ֖ת עֶרְוַ֥ת מִצְרָֽיִם׃

i18n.en: so shall the king of Assyria lead away the captives of Egypt and the exiles of Cush, young and old, naked and barefoot, and with buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt.
i18n.he: כֵּ֣ן יִנְהַ֣ג מֶֽלֶךְ־אַ֠שּׁוּר אֶת־שְׁבִ֨י מִצְרַ֜יִם וְאֶת־גָּל֥וּת כּ֛וּשׁ נְעָרִ֥ים וּזְקֵנִ֖ים עָר֣וֹם וְיָחֵ֑ף וַחֲשׂוּפַ֥י שֵׁ֖ת עֶרְוַ֥ת מִצְרָֽיִם׃

notes.official:
*Waḥăśûp̄ay šēṯ* “with buttocks uncovered” follows ASV and JPS 1917; NJPS has “with bared buttocks.” *Ḥăśûp̄ay* is a construct plural of the passive participle of *ḥśp* “strip, lay bare” with an anomalous ending in *-ay* where *ḥăśûp̄ê* is expected. The grammars treat it either as a relic of an older ending or as a scribal error (GKC; recalled, section not verified). *Šēṯ* “seat, buttocks” is rare. The plural is used of the Ammonite humiliation of David’s envoys, whose garments were cut “to their buttocks” (2 Sam 10:4; ASV checked).

*ʿErwaṯ miṣrāyim* stands in apposition, literally “the nakedness of Egypt.” *ʿErwāh* is nakedness as exposure and disgrace (Gen 9:22–23; Lam 1:8). ASV, JPS 1917 and NJPS all render “to the shame of Egypt,” and the line keeps that wording. The central entry `ervat-aviv` is not extended, because it governs the Genesis idiom “the nakedness of his father.” *Šᵉḇî* “captives” and *gālûṯ* “exiles” are the usual nouns for deportees. *Nᵉʿārîm ûzᵉqēnîm* “young and old” is a merism: the whole population.

paragraphs.translit: kēn yinhag melek-ʾaššūr ʾet-šəbī miṣrayim wəʾet-gālūt kūš nəʿārīm ūzəqēnīm ʿārōm wəyāḥēp waḥăśūpay šēt ʿerwat miṣrāyim

paragraphs.text: וְחַתּ֖וּ וָבֹ֑שׁוּ מִכּוּשׁ֙ מַבָּטָ֔ם וּמִן־מִצְרַ֖יִם תִּפְאַרְתָּֽם׃

i18n.en: And they shall be dismayed and ashamed because of Cush their expectation, and of Egypt their honor.
i18n.he: וְחַתּ֖וּ וָבֹ֑שׁוּ מִכּוּשׁ֙ מַבָּטָ֔ם וּמִן־מִצְרַ֖יִם תִּפְאַרְתָּֽם׃

notes.official:
*Tip̄ʾartām* is “their honor,” the book’s default for *tip̄ʾereṯ* (overlay `tsemach-yhwh-branch-isaiah-4`, extended here). That default keeps “glory” for *kāḇôḏ* under wave I-4 ruling 2. ASV and JPS 1917 have “their glory” and NJPS has “their boast.” Here the noun is what the people prided themselves on, the power they leaned on. 10:12 records the departure “boasting” for *tip̄ʾereṯ*, where the noun is the Assyrian king’s arrogance and “honor” would not fit. At 20:5 the idiom allows “honor,” so the default stands, and NJPS’s “boast” is given here as the nearest English sense.

*Mabbāṭ*, “that to which one looks,” is “expectation” with ASV and JPS 1917 (NJPS “hope”). It is rendered the same way here and at 20:6, so that the repetition shows. The pairing is chiastic: Cush the hope and Egypt the boast, reversing the order of 20:4. *Wᵉḥattû wāḇōšû* is “they shall be dismayed and ashamed” (JPS 1917; ASV “confounded”). The subject is not expressed. It is most naturally the people of “this coastland” in 20:6, the Philistine cities, and perhaps Judah, which looked to the same help. The English leaves it as “they,” as in the Hebrew.

paragraphs.translit: wəḥattū wābōšū mikkūš mabbāṭām ūmin-miṣrayim tipʾartām

paragraphs.text: וְ֠אָמַר יֹשֵׁ֨ב הָאִ֣י הַזֶּה֮ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַהוּא֒ הִנֵּה־כֹ֣ה מַבָּטֵ֗נוּ אֲשֶׁר־נַ֤סְנוּ שָׁם֙ לְעֶזְרָ֔ה לְהִ֨נָּצֵ֔ל מִפְּנֵ֖י מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֑וּר וְאֵ֖יךְ נִמָּלֵ֥ט אֲנָֽחְנוּ׃ (ס)

i18n.en: And the inhabitant of this coastland shall say in that day: ‘Behold, such is our expectation, where we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria; and we, how shall we escape?’”
i18n.he: וְ֠אָמַר יֹשֵׁ֨ב הָאִ֣י הַזֶּה֮ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַהוּא֒ הִנֵּה־כֹ֣ה מַבָּטֵ֗נוּ אֲשֶׁר־נַ֤סְנוּ שָׁם֙ לְעֶזְרָ֔ה לְהִ֨נָּצֵ֔ל מִפְּנֵ֖י מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֑וּר וְאֵ֖יךְ נִמָּלֵ֥ט אֲנָֽחְנוּ׃ (ס)

notes.official:
*Yōšēḇ hāʾî hazzeh* “the inhabitant of this coastland”: *ʾî* covers both coast and island (BDB). The book renders *ʾî / ʾiyyîm* “coastland(s)” (11:11; 24:15; 42:4), and the extension of overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-11` records the concordance here. ASV and JPS 1917 have “coast-land” and NJPS “coastland.” In context it is the Philistine coast, where Ashdod stands (20:1). The singular *yōšēḇ* is a collective. The line keeps “the inhabitant” with ASV and JPS 1917, and NJPS renders “the dwellers.”

*Hinnēh-ḵōh mabbāṭēnû* “Behold, such is our expectation” is ASV’s literal rendering. NJPS paraphrases it: “If this could happen to those we looked to.” The closing *wᵉʾêḵ nimmālēṭ ʾănāḥnû* places the pronoun last for emphasis, “and we, how shall we escape?” (ASV). The inner quotation ends YHWH’s speech, which opened at 20:3.

paragraphs.translit: wəʾāmar yōšēb hāʾī hazzeh bayyōm hahūʾ hinnēh-kōh mabbāṭēnū ʾăšer-nasnū šām ləʿezrāh ləhinnāṣēl mippənê melek ʾaššūr wəʾêk nimmālēṭ ʾănāḥnū
